downside.title: Quick check: your downside
downside.prompt: You put $1,000 into a stock. Right after, the price falls 10%. What is your position worth now?
downside.explain_correct: Yes. A 10% fall on $1,000 is $100, so you hold $900. The loss comes off your money the moment the price falls, and you only turn it into cash if you sell.
downside.explain_wrong: Not quite. The price fell, so your shares are worth less: 10% of $1,000 is $100, leaving $900. You only turn that into cash if you sell.
downside.pitch_label: worked out their downside after one simulated trade

safety_net.title: Quick check: the safety net
safety_net.prompt: You set a safety net (a stop-loss) 10% below your purchase price. Then the price keeps falling. What does the safety net do?
options: It sells my shares automatically once the price hits my stop, which limits how much more I can lose.
It buys more shares to lower my average price.
safety_net.explain_correct: Yes. It limits your loss; it does not erase it. And if the price dips to your stop and bounces back, you were sold out at the bottom. That is the price of protection.
safety_net.explain_wrong: Not quite. A safety net sells your shares automatically once the price falls to your stop, so a fall cannot keep hurting you. You still take the loss up to that point, and it cannot buy anything for you.
